extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, critics, and practitioners of drama/playwriting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging tragic drama, focusing on the primacy of plot (action) over character, the nature of dramatic conflict, unity and causality, and how character should be manifested through action. Draws on Aristotelian Poetics and comparative examples (Greek, Shakespeare, moderns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as first principle / soul of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The plot is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.’ A play is an imitation not of men but of action; life consists in action and its end is a mode of action, not a quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the animating principle from which the parts grow and group themselves; it is the origin of movement, the starting-point and basis of the play. To judge a tragedy, evaluate whether the plot gives the play its inner meaning and realises its intention. Examples/explanation: plot contains decisive moments (reversals) that awaken tragic feeling; without a coherent plot a tragedy cannot exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be exhibited developmentally and causally
rubrics_metrics.description: Action, to be dramatic, must be exhibited in its development and in its results; it must stand in reciprocal and causal relation to certain mental states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether deeds arise from motives and lead to consequences in a coherent causal chain (a complete whole). Mere isolated deeds, however terrible, are not dramatic unless shown as part of a causal sequence tied to emotion/will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters are subsidiary to actions (dramatic character defined by action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character determines men's qualities, but it is by their actions that they are happy or the reverse. Dramatic action is not with a view to the representation of character: character comes in as subsidiary to the actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters by how they function within the action: do they produce, further, or respond to events? Characters that do not influence the plot are of little dramatic value; character should be revealed through action rather than through detached portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama cannot lack plot (but can lack detailed character-portraiture)
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a tragedy without character; there cannot be a tragedy without action. 'From this point of view it may be said that you can have a drama without “character,” but not without “plot.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work possesses a central action even if character-drawing is minimal (types or class characteristics may suffice if action is strong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict is the soul of the drama and must manifest outwardly
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic conflict, not the mere plot, is 'the soul of a tragedy.' In every drama there is a collision of forces; this conflict must manifest itself in individual acts and concrete relations with the world outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude inward-only struggles as dramatic unless they are brought into concrete actions and collisions with other wills. Assess whether the conflict produces outward deeds and interactions, not just internal rumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal mental activity must be externalised to be dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely mental conflicts—action and reaction within the mind itself—are dramatic only when they are brought into a plot which gives them significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that intellectual or speculative thought has outward consequences or is translated into deeds; solitary inward action alone is generally undramatic (anti-pattern: drama of motionless life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dianoia / dialectical reasoning should serve the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under dianoia are included the intellectual reflexions of the speaker: the proof of his own statements, the disproof of those of his opponents, his general maxims concerning life and conduct, as elicited by the action and forming part of a train of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reasoning and moralizing speech by whether it advances the action or elucidates motives. The book connects dialectical dianoia with political/forensic influences on the drama; such speech must be integral to the ἀγών of the play, not mere ethical monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must possess will/energetic force to produce action
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic character has some vital and spontaneous force which can make and mould circumstances, which sets obstacles aside. The emotions must harden into will and the will express itself in deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for 'battling, energetic' characters whose impulses become deeds. Passive characters fit lyrical poetry rather than drama (exceptions like Hamlet’s intellectual inaction are rare and special).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and organic structure of the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic action forms a complete whole: it is a coherent series of events, standing in organic relation to one another and bound together by the law of cause and effect. The internal centre, the pivot round which the whole system turns, is the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess unity of beginning, middle, end; whether all parts grow round the central plot and contribute to the appointed end. The plot should not feel a collection of disconnected episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/necessity (causal inevitability) in plot construction
rubrics_metrics.description: An inner bond of probability or necessity binds events together. The fate that overtakes the hero is no alien thing, but his own self put upon him for good or evil. 'Man's character... is his destiny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether events follow plausibly (by character and circumstance) rather than by arbitrary chance; the element of chance should be largely eliminated in a well-constructed tragic plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reversals and decisive moments (peripeteia/anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot... contains those Reversals of the Situation (epimérecac) and other decisive moments, which most powerfully awaken tragic feeling and excite the pleasure appropriate to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and placement of reversals/recognitions that alter situation and heighten tragic emotion; these moments should be organically motivated by the plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot complication for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: In maintaining that plot is the first essential of the drama, it is not implied that the plot must be complicated... Not even in Oedipus is dramatic complication an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of mechanism or convoluted puzzles that merely tangle and untangle to excite curiosity; prefer coherent, meaningful structure rather than artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos (character/ethical portraiture) must derive meaning through form/plot
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The most beautiful colours, laid on confusedly, will not give as much pleasure as the chalk outline of a portrait.’ Ethos divorced from plot is like a daub of beautiful colour, which apart from form gives little pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ethical portraiture and character traits are integrated into the dramatic form; isolated moralizing or aesthetic presentation without structural function is ineffective (anti-pattern: beautiful but formless monologues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should often embody universal principles (type and universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek tragedy dramatises the play of great principles... The heroes are themselves the concrete embodiment of these forces. The characters thereby gain universal meaning and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether characters, while particular, express wider social/moral realities (patriotism, family duty, law) so that the play attains universal significance rather than only local or idiosyncratic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and temporal framing for character development
rubrics_metrics.description: The romantic (modern) drama aimed at a more comprehensive representation; as the period embraced by the action is extended... characters expand and undergo essential changes; the moderns follow character growth through successive stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For longer-scope dramas, evaluate how well extended time and antecedent material are incorporated to show organic development; when scope is enlarged, ensure unity and causal coherence remain intact (avoid turning drama into mere dramatic biography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude drama of 'motionless life' unless transmuted into action
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to the merely statuesque, to motionless life... If lyrical utterance remained dominant the tragic drama would be left to others. Drama of motionless life beguiles some men to heresy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware works that glorify inward feeling or static tableau without translating feeling into willful deeds; such static drama is typically undramatic unless the speeches function directly as action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters reveal personality only as required by the action
rubrics_metrics.description: They reveal their personality not in all its fulness, but to such an extent as the natural course of the action may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the presentation of character is proportionate to dramatic needs—excessive backstory or exhaustive psychological portraiting that does not serve action can weaken dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual/reflexive speeches must function as steps in the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Each speech of Prometheus is a step in the action; each word he utters is equivalent to a deed. The dialogue is translated into deed, and culminates in a tragic catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether expository or reflective speeches advance the plot, change relations, or effect outcomes; if not, they risk being undramatic ethical monologues (anti-pattern).
